column1: Mimicking

Can Putin recruit North Koreans to fight in Ukraine? In the wake of this burgeoning alliance, speculation swirls like a persistent mist. Will the notoriously isolated nation of North Korea, under the iron fist of Kim Jong-un, truly send its troops to Ukraine’s battle-scarred fields? The whispers of such a pact intensify, as the specter of a resurgent, albeit morally dubious, Axis looms. The potential consequences are myriad, etching a grim tableau of global instability. It’s a precarious game, with the lives of ordinary people as pawns on a geopolitical chessboard. One can almost envision the scenarios playing out in the halls of power, where cynical calculations weigh the cost of human lives against the allure of territorial gains. While Putin's ambition knows no bounds, there seems to be always a catch. This time, the stakes are higher, and the game more perilous than ever. Could this be the genesis of a new Cold War, or something even more sinister? Only the relentless march of time will unveil the truth, however, the picture of the future seems bleak.

Where is Putin’s bunker located? Vladimir Putin has multiple bunkers. It seems, though, none of those is good enough for the paranoid ruler, who feels the need to always hide. First, let’s recall the rumors regarding the “deep state” and the “globalists” that Putin’s propagandists have been feeding to the Russian public since day one. The deep state, the elites, the cabal—they all are planning something treacherous against the great Putin. Given this narrative, it comes as no surprise that one of Putin's primary obsessions is personal safety, and thus, the construction of underground bunkers, which are supposed to withstand a nuclear attack. It's an open secret that Putin's paranoia has reached epic proportions, yet he's strangely unconcerned about the safety of his own people. While he's busy building lavish bunkers, his citizens are left to suffer in crumbling infrastructure, with no access to adequate healthcare, facing the daily realities of their bleak existence. Of course, the existence of such a bunker is secret, yet there are reports.

Do Russians prefer Marine Le Pen over Emmanuel Macron in the upcoming French presidential election? Just 8 days ago, Russia’s RIA Novosti was gleefully celebrating, “Marine Le Pen buried Emmanuel Macron.” Last night, the Russian news were at a loss, not knowing how to comment on the fact that Marine Le Pen’s party lost not only to Macron’s centric alliance, but got beaten by the leftist “Popular Front”. The Kremlin didn’t prepare instructions for propagandists for such a case. But it was fixed overnight, and the Kremlin spin sounds as “France is finished”. In Kremlin’s version, it’s not Marine Le Pen that is “finished”, but the whole big country of France. Kremlin propagandists accused Macron in disregarding “the expression of the people’s will” — yes, this comes from the country where any opinion against the government gets you either in jail or grave — depending on Putin’s mood in the morning. An interesting background on Marine Le Pen is that her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was a co-founder of the far-right party she was representing in the last 2 French presidential elections. The “National Front” party, which initially included Nazi-era collaborators, had been convicted multiple times for antisemitic hate speech and described the Holocaust as “a detail” of WWII history. However, in 2002, Le Pen Senior advanced into the 2nd round of presidential stand off against Jacques Chirac. That was the moment in French electoral history where the terrified French voters said, “Non!”, overwhelmingly rejecting Le Pen, with even the fans of the left voting to put Chirac, a conservative, in the Elysee Palace. Since then, French political parties used the tactic consistently against the far-right. The same strategy helped to consolidate centrist and leftist voters in the July 7 snap parliamentary elections, when Le Pen’s party only scored the 3rd, behind the leftist coalition and Macron’s alliance. Marine Le Pen’s father, who is now 96, left the big politics 13 years ago, in 2011. His party never won presidential elections. Following in his footsteps, Marine Le Pen participated in 2012, 2017 and 2022 presidential elections, losing them all. After her loss in 2022 presidential elections, Marine Le Pen handed the leadership to 26-year-old Jordan Bardella. He became the first person without the Le Pen name to lead the “National Front” since its founding in 1972. On the campaign trail, Le Pen and Bardella have presented themselves as “running mates”, with Le Pen vying for the presidency while pushing her protege for the position of prime minister. Obviously, Russian propagandists didn’t see Bardella as a proper leader, continuing to refer to Marine Le Pen as the leading force in the party. Yes, the leaders of the Russian regime are bitterly disappointed that Le Pen’s party didn’t win — they have already purchased expensive French champagne to celebrate (and its not a figure of speech — Google “Russians drink champagne for Donald Trump’s victory”). But they are hopeful that the leader of the leftist party that scored the majority of seats in the parliament will also interfere with France’s participation in NATO and especially with helping Ukraine. The hope expressed by pro-Putin commentators under the posts about Le Pen’s party loss is that “Melenchon will be even worse for Ukraine”, which means automatically, it will be better for Russia. 72-year-old Jean-Luc Mélenchon is a founder of left-wing ‘France Unbowed’ party. He became the self-appointed figurehead of the alliance comprised of — in addition to his own party — the Socialist Party, the French Communist Party as well as green, center-left and left-wing political groups, which scored the most number of seats in the parliamentary elections. The Russian propagandists keep their hopes up. Then, there’s the ever-present spectre of the “West” — that amorphous, nebulous entity that serves as the ultimate boogeyman in the Kremlin's narrative. Any setback for the West, any crack in its perceived unity, is cause for unbridled elation in Moscow. And France, with its rich history, powerful economy, and pivotal role in European affairs, is a prime target for this kind of gleeful opportunism. The Russian media, controlled entirely by the state, never misses an opportunity to exploit divisions, amplify dissent, and generally sow discord. They have honed this skill to a fine art, and the ongoing French political imbroglio is a veritable field day for them. It's all part of a bigger game, a relentless campaign to undermine the West from within. And, as history has repeatedly shown, it's a game the Kremlin is all too willing to play.

Does Russia have any Red Dawn type movies showing an American invasion? Russians are too scared to make movies where the Americans are shown as a formidable foe. Instead, they tend to depict them as buffoonish characters, lacking any real substance or threat. Consider, for instance, the recent series announced by Russia's TNT channel, poised to chronicle the escapades of Joe Biden on Russian soil. Billed as a comedy, the premise revolves around the American president embarking on an incognito trip to Russia, ostensibly to unravel the mystery behind the ineffectiveness of sanctions. The script paints a picture of Biden losing his documents, shackled to a cramped apartment reminiscent of the Khrushchev era, moonlighting as an English teacher, and forging an unlikely bond with a quintessential “true Russian patriot.” The series, bearing the title “Goodbye,” promises a “kind, true-to-life, funny story,” according to the actor Dmitry Dyuzhev, who is set to portray the US president. Dyuzhev, it should be noted, previously graced the screen portraying a pregnant man. In the stark reality of politics, however, "Sleepy Joe" has consistently outmaneuvered Putin, delivering a series of strategic victories. And now, in what seems like a retaliatory move, Russian television aims to lampoon the US president. The Russian film industry is, quite frankly, a shadow of its former self. Anyone daring to view reality through anything other than Putin's distorted lens has either fled the country or been silenced. Those remaining have resigned themselves to churning out propaganda, dictated by the ideologues within the presidential administration. Even within this carefully constructed world of propaganda, the notion of America invading Russia, or indeed any foreign power successfully invading the country, is simply too preposterous for Putin's underlings to contemplate. You won’t find any movies of that ilk. The only cinematic forays into foreign invasions tend to be relegated to the annals of World War II or other relics of history.

How good is Putin in using nationalism or patriotism for his gain? Since 2022, Putin and his propagandists promote the idea of dying to get more land for Russia as the most important thing for any citizen. At first, Putin was blunt, stating to mothers of soldiers that it’s better for their sons to die in Ukraine from shrapnel wounds or bullets than from drinking bootleg alcohol or in a car crash. Then in 2023, propagandist Vladimir Solovyov (who might soon get an arrest warrant from Hague international court for crimes against humanity — for his bloodthirsty propaganda rants) was insisting one shouldn’t be afraid of death. “Life is greatly overrated,” Solovyov proclaimed on state TV to the audience of millions. “Life is greatly overrated. Why be afraid of what is inevitable?” Solovyov was trying to be convincing. Now Putin calls for Russians to volunteer to go to war, without sparing their lives and health, stating that’s what patriotism is. (Video in the comments below.) Apparently, the only problem Putin has — he can’t find the right words, which would convince Russian men to do it. He's trying hard. Yet, the results of his "patriotic" efforts are rather lackluster. He is facing a severe shortage of manpower, with those willing to fight dwindling and the ones being conscripted actively fleeing the country. Meanwhile, a Russian soldier says that things in Putin’s army aren’t great at all. The recruiters are happy to send to the front anyone — aged, crippled, unprepared, and drug addicts. The attitude of the commanders is terrible: “They just throw in as meat those without an eye, without fingers…” This is patriotism “Russian style”, young man. The more suffering, the more death, the more patriotic citizen of mother Russia you are. Putin’s “patriotic” agenda reveals itself: instead of a glorious victory, Russia is experiencing the collapse of its army, with many soldiers forced into the conflict against their will or without proper training. If the war against Ukraine continues for a long time, Vladimir Putin will learn the hard way that a nation cannot be built on nationalism and cynicism, and for sure, Vladimir Putin did not understand this.

What are Vladimir Putin's ambitions in Ukraine, and what was he trying to accomplish there? For years, the West has been trying to figure out what Vladimir Putin wants. Is his end goal the recreation of the Soviet Union? Or perhaps, as some analysts suggest, is it simply to restore the Russian Empire to its former glory, or at least, to its pre-1917 borders? Some even suggest a more narrow focus: control over Ukraine and its resources. The man himself isn't exactly forthcoming with the details. Publicly, Putin has offered a string of justifications for his actions, each one seeming to shift and change with the tides of war, but always tinged with a heavy dose of historical revisionism.  First and foremost, Putin has claimed he is "denazifying" Ukraine. This assertion is, to put it mildly, ludicrous, given that the Ukrainian president is Jewish and democratically elected. This talking point, a favorite of Kremlin propagandists, is often used to paint the Ukrainian government as illegitimate and to garner support from a populace with a deep historical aversion to Nazism. Then there's the matter of NATO expansion. Moscow argues that the West has sought to encroach on its sphere of influence, and that Ukraine's westward leanings pose a direct threat to Russia’s security. However, the fact is that NATO is a defensive alliance, and there is no credible evidence of any imminent invasion from the West. Furthermore, Ukraine expressed its desire to join the EU and NATO back in 2014 after the Euromaidan revolution. It was the end of Russian dominance over the country after the Ukrainian people ousted Putin’s puppet, Viktor Yanukovych, signaling the beginning of the end of Russian control over Ukraine.  Beyond these public pronouncements, it is reasonable to speculate what Putin is truly after. One of the primary goals seems to be the complete subjugation of Ukraine. He seeks to install a puppet regime that would be beholden to the Kremlin, and to strip Ukraine of its sovereignty and its national identity. A secondary goal appears to be to weaken the West, particularly the United States and the European Union, by sowing discord, creating chaos, and exhausting resources in a prolonged military conflict. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has already exposed the divisions within NATO and the EU, testing the limits of their unity when threatened by the actions of a modern-day autocrat. Finally, Putin is likely motivated by a desire to secure his legacy. By projecting an image of strength and resolve, of a leader who is willing to stand up to the West and restore Russia to its former glory, he hopes to cement his place in history. Whether he succeeds in these ambitious goals is another question altogether. The war has backfired spectacularly, and the once-feared Russian military is now bogged down in a bloody struggle that is likely to consume the regime itself.

If Vladimir Putin learned he only had a few weeks to live, would he nuke the USA? The question itself is a morbid thought experiment, the kind that fuels late-night conversations fueled by cheap vodka, or, perhaps, high-brow philosophical debates in dimly lit university halls. Could a man, stripped of the illusion of immortality that most leaders cling to, resort to such a catastrophic act? Considering Putin's track record, the answer is not straightforward. The rumors surrounding his health, the way he isolates himself, the level of control he exerts – all paint a picture of a man terrified of the unknown. But fear, as any student of history will tell you, can manifest in unpredictable ways.  On one hand, the meticulously crafted image of the strongman, impervious to weakness, might crumble under the weight of mortality. The carefully constructed narrative of Russia's resurgence could be shattered, leaving him with nothing but ashes and a legacy of ruin. In such a scenario, a final, desperate act of destruction, a "go down with the ship" mentality, wouldn’t be entirely out of character. It would be, in a twisted way, a final assertion of power, a declaration that if he couldn't have the world, no one could.  However, there's another, equally plausible, interpretation. Putin isn't just a dictator; he's a pragmatist. He understands the delicate balance of power, the terrifying implications of nuclear war. He’s cultivated an image not just of strength, but also of strategic brilliance. He understands consequences more than most, given his history of KGB training. Launching a nuclear strike would not only obliterate the United States but would also condemn Russia to annihilation. It’s a move that wouldn't be about power itself, but sheer madness.

How is the Russian economy doing? What kind of data has its economy produced in recent months, positive or negative? Official sources in Russia keep releasing upbeat statistics, painting a rosy picture of a thriving economy. The rosy tint, though, is likely to be a clever manipulation of facts, if not outright lies. One must treat everything coming out of the Kremlin with extreme skepticism, as their credibility is in tatters. Recent reports suggest a significant rise in industrial production, claiming it's indicative of robust economic growth. However, a closer examination reveals a different reality, obscured by the fog of propaganda. Much of this supposed “growth” is fueled by the military-industrial complex, churning out weapons and equipment for the war in Ukraine, rather than addressing the needs of its citizenry. Consumer spending remains stagnant, if not worse, and real wages continue to decline. This disparity highlights the chasm between the Kremlin’s narrative and the lived experiences of ordinary Russians. Inflation is eating away at people's savings, and the sanctions imposed by the West are biting harder with each passing month, further exacerbating the situation. While the Russian government is adept at creating an illusion of stability, the underlying economic fundamentals are fragile at best, and on the verge of collapse at their worst. It's a house of cards, propped up by increasingly desperate measures, with the potential to crumble at any moment. The long-term consequences of diverting resources to a senseless war—instead of investing in the well-being of the Russian people—are already becoming painfully apparent.

What is happening in the Kursk region of Russia? Last week, the Kursk region, bordering Ukraine, was struck by a series of drone attacks. The regional governor, Roman Starovoit, promptly reported the incidents, though details remained scarce. He initially characterized the assaults as targeting infrastructure, notably power lines, and, predictably, blamed Kyiv. Starovoit, a staunch Putin loyalist, has consistently toed the Kremlin line, often echoing the official narrative with remarkable alacrity. The response was immediate and, in true Russian fashion, centered on reinforcing existing security measures rather than critically assessing potential vulnerabilities. This reactive approach is, sadly, a hallmark of the current regime, forever putting out fires without addressing the underlying causes. The nature and origin of these drones remain a subject of intense speculation. Some reports suggest Ukrainian involvement, while others posit internal sabotage or even deliberate provocations orchestrated by Moscow itself—a tactic to further consolidate existing tensions. One can’t deny the potential for such a cynical maneuver, given the Kremlin’s penchant for manufacturing pretexts to justify its actions, as the Kursk region is strategically significant, closely situated near the Ukrainian border.

Why does the current Russian military seem so incompetent? The ineptitude of the Russian military, as demonstrated in the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, is a source of bewilderment. It's a stark contrast to the image meticulously crafted by Russian propaganda over the years, depicting a formidable, almost invincible fighting force. The reality, however, is far more… complicated, and, frankly, embarrassing for the Kremlin. The issues seem to stem from several interconnected factors, a veritable Gordian knot of failures that have hamstrung their operations.  Corruption, for one, is a malignant tumor that has metastasized throughout the entire system. The pilfering of funds, the embezzlement of resources, the shady deals – all these practices have eroded the military's ability to function effectively. Equipment is substandard, supplies are inadequate, and the morale of the troops is in the gutter. Moreover, the quality of leadership appears sorely lacking. Commanders are seemingly chosen for their loyalty to Putin, not their strategic acumen or battlefield experience. This results in poor decision-making, reckless tactics, and a staggering disregard for the lives of Russian soldiers. The focus seems to be less on winning and more on maintaining control, a symptom of the broader authoritarian grip on power. This breeds a culture of fear and silence, where criticism is swiftly punished and incompetence is rewarded, perpetuating a cycle of failure. The initial planning for the invasion was shockingly naive, a gamble that has backfired spectacularly. The subsequent adjustments, characterized by brutal assaults, heavy losses, and a dependence on outdated strategies, suggest a military struggling to adapt to the realities of modern warfare. Indeed, the whole debacle is a monumental embarrassment, a tragedy of epic proportions, and a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of unchecked power and endemic corruption. It is a story of hubris, miscalculations, and the tragically unavoidable consequences of incompetence on a grand scale.

Why doesn't the pro-Russian crowd realize that Macgreggor and Scott Ritter simply aren't reliable sources of information, AT ALL? The answer, as plain as day, appears to be a complex tapestry woven with threads of delusion, perhaps even willful ignorance. The echo chamber of pro-Putin sentiment, it seems, is impervious to logic, to truth, to any semblance of verifiable facts. It's a self-perpetuating cycle, where flawed narratives are embraced, and any dissenting voices are promptly dismissed, often with barely a second thought. One wonders if this unwavering allegiance stems from a deep-seated fear of the unknown. The fear to question what they've been told. The fear of confronting the stark realities of the situation. Or perhaps, it's simply a blind faith, a devotion to a charismatic leader who, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, is still perceived as the savior of a crumbling empire. Macgreggor and Ritter, in this context, function not as purveyors of truth, but as comforting voices, validating pre-existing beliefs, reinforcing the desired narrative. The details, the inconsistencies, the obvious biases – all these are conveniently overlooked, for the sake of clinging to a belief system. It’s a dangerous game they’re playing, a game where the stakes are not only truth and integrity, but the very future of their country, a country now under the looming shadow of a dictator who seems to be determined to drag everyone down with himself.

In Russia, did the video of the effeminate Russian soldiers surrendering to the manly Ukraine army make them embarrassed? The answer is: yes. The video likely caused significant consternation within Russia, and its effects were widely discussed. It's quite probable that many Russians felt a complex mixture of emotions, including shame, anger, and a profound sense of humiliation. The images of their soldiers, often portrayed as paragons of strength and masculinity, yielding to Ukrainian forces directly contradicted the state-sponsored narrative of invincibility. The very essence of Putin's propaganda, carefully constructed to bolster national pride and project an image of military superiority, was undermined in an instant. The perception of weakness, particularly in the context of a war that was supposed to be a swift operation, would have been a bitter pill to swallow for many, especially those who believed the hype. The carefully cultivated image of the "strong Russian man," so central to the Kremlin's messaging, took a brutal hit. This narrative was carefully constructed to contrast the allegedly weak, decadent West with a strong, traditional Russia. Therefore, the sight of their own soldiers surrendering would have hit particularly hard. The impact, I suspect, reverberated through the social media, especially the pro-war channels, with the desperate search for explanations and the frantic attempts to spin the embarrassing reality. The Kremlin's reaction, likely, would have been swift.

Putin finally backpedalled and offered his desire to handshake with Ukraine. Can we deduce that he finally realised the West's firm resoluteness against his aggressive behaviours in the past over two years, thus extending the olive branch to Ukraine? Or – is it merely a tactical maneuver, a calculated play in a game of geopolitical chess fueled by desperation? Frankly, with Putin, it’s always a gamble, a high-stakes poker game where the stakes are nations and the cards are lies meticulously crafted to deceive. We’ve seen these theatrics before, the fleeting peace overtures that vanish quicker than a mirage in the desert sun. This sudden display of camaraderie, of a willingness to extend a hand, feels particularly suspect, especially given the mounting evidence of Russia's military setbacks and economic woes. The Kremlin is facing an increasingly uphill battle, a complex web of sanctions, military failures, and the slowly awakening world opinion. Could this be the sign of a genuine shift, a genuine shift towards negotiation and compromise? Or, with the distinct whiff of a desperate ploy to buy time, regroup, and reload, before launching another offensive when the world's attention is diverted? It's likely the latter. Putin's playbook is as predictable as it is ruthless: destabilization, disinformation, and destruction – the only real change in play is in the execution. The man is a master strategist, a Machiavellian puppeteer pulling the strings of a global stage, and we are merely the audience. This olive branch? Expect it to be a poisoned one.

Does the world know the Kursk offensive was nothing more than a PR stunt by Ukraine, in order to manufacture some type of hope for more funding? The audacity of such a claim is staggering, a testament to the convoluted narratives spun to justify the unjustifiable. It’s a narrative strategy ripped straight from the Kremlin’s playbook: sow doubt, confuse the audience, and undermine the truth. To suggest the Kursk offensive was a mere "stunt" – a theatrical production designed to solicit financial aid – is not just a distortion of reality, it's an insult to the sacrifices made and the lives irrevocably altered.   It’s a classic example of propaganda, where facts are twisted to fit a predetermined conclusion. One can only speculate on where this originates from, but it’s clear that its objective is to delegitimize Ukraine's struggle and erode international support. The sheer disregard for human lives and suffering, the cynical exploitation of a devastating conflict - it's all too familiar. This manipulative tactic attempts to portray Ukraine as a deceptive actor, shifting the blame from the aggressor to the victim. The architects of this misinformation campaign fail to grasp that the truth, however painful, always prevails.

What is it like to live in Cuba? Cuba, a land steeped in revolutionary fervor, stands apart, a paradox wrapped in a tight embargo. Imagine a place where the vibrant vestiges of a bygone era mingle with the realities of a socialist state. The iconic vintage cars, a testament to ingenuity born of necessity, cruise the sun-drenched streets, alongside crumbling facades whispering tales of grandeur and decline. Life in Cuba is a captivating blend of resilience and resourcefulness; a daily negotiation between the dreams of a better tomorrow and the constraints of the present.  One might get the sense that time has somehow stopped in Cuba. The rhythm of daily life moves at a decidedly slower pace, punctuated not by the relentless tick-tock of capitalist efficiency but by the melodic cadence of Spanish chatter, the aroma of strong Cuban coffee, and the infectious beat of salsa. The palpable joy in shared experiences is the true currency here, and the simple act of exchanging a smile can feel like a lavish gift. However, this idyllic portrayal overlays a complex reality: the persistent struggle to satisfy basic needs, limited access to information, and a palpable tension between the ideals of the revolution and the realities of the market. Cubans have mastered the art of making do, improvising, and finding beauty amidst hardship. They’ve learned to navigate the maze of restrictions with a unique blend of wit, spirit, and unwavering hope. The Cuban spirit, a force of nature itself, endures, making life in Cuba a remarkable and thought-provoking experience, one that leaves a lasting impression on anyone fortunate enough to witness its unique charm. The stories of these people are a testament to the indomitable spirit of humankind, thriving even under the crushing weight of circumstance.

Which country has better military technology, Ukraine or Russia/USSR? Since the beginning of the full-scale war in Ukraine, we've been bombarded with claims about military might, technological supremacy, and the effectiveness of various weapons systems. The reality, as always, is far more nuanced.  Initially, the narrative painted a picture of a technologically superior Russian army, laden with advanced weaponry. However, the battlefield has revealed a different story. While Russia undoubtedly possesses some impressive military hardware, its effectiveness has been repeatedly hampered by logistical failures, poor training, and questionable tactical decisions. The Russian military, at least during the first year of the war, appeared to be fighting on a shoestring, with basic equipment and outdated supply chains.  Conversely, Ukraine, despite being significantly outmatched in terms of sheer numbers and overall resources, has demonstrated a remarkable ability to utilize Western-supplied weaponry effectively. The Ukrainians have shown extraordinary ingenuity and adaptability in employing these systems, turning the tide of battle on multiple occasions. They’ve mastered the art of asymmetric warfare. The use of drones, for instance, has been a game-changer, with both sides adopting them on a massive scale.  It's not just about the technology itself but also about how it's utilized. The Russians, often hampered by bureaucracy and rigid hierarchies, have struggled to adapt to the ever-changing battlefield reality. The Ukrainians, by contrast, have demonstrated a level of flexibility and innovation that has allowed them to maximize the effectiveness of the weapons they have.  It’s a brutal, bloody conflict, no matter how advanced or primitive the weaponry. The war has shown that military technology alone doesn't guarantee victory; it is a whole picture, starting from a strong army, continuing with good training, excellent coordination, and brave soldiers. And let’s not forget the motivation to fight.  In terms of the USSR, the question becomes even more complex, as the Soviet Union, at its peak, boasted a military-industrial complex that was arguably on par with, if not surpassing, its Western counterparts. However, the collapse of the Soviet Union led to a decline in military capabilities for all former Soviet republics, included Russia. Many of the technologies of the USSR are in the museums now.

Is it true that Vladimir Putin brought a Labrador to a meeting with Angela Merkel because she's afraid of dogs? This juicy tidbit, like so many from the Kremlin, is multifaceted. The story itself is probably apocryphal, a delightful blend of rumor and speculation. But the very fact that it circulates, that it has legs in the media, is far more telling than the veracity of the anecdote itself. The subtext of the narrative is clear: Putin, the master strategist, understands the weaknesses of his opponents and, with a carefully orchestrated gesture, exploits them. Merkel, the iron lady, rendered vulnerable by a simple four-legged creature? It plays into the grand narrative of Putin as a cunning, almost Machiavellian, political actor. The reality, as with most things emanating from the Russian leadership, is undoubtedly more intricate and less theatrical. Still, the image has value. The story, like any good propaganda, works on multiple levels, appealing to various audiences. Some find it amusing, a bit of harmless political gossip. Others see it as evidence of Putin's ruthlessly tactical approach to international relations. Regardless of the truth, the widespread dissemination of such stories underscores a key element of the Kremlin's playbook: the manipulation of perception.

Why do you think Russia was neither invited nor recognised as a genuine peace initiative for the Global Peace Summit? It’s a rather pertinent question, isn’t it? Considering the current geopolitical landscape, the conspicuous absence of Russia from the Global Peace Summit, and the lack of recognition of any proffered "peace initiatives" speaks volumes. The narrative of this conflict, as it's being shaped and disseminated, is one where Russia is painted as the aggressor, the instigator of turmoil, and therefore, unfit to be a credible peacemaker. This framing, meticulously crafted and amplified by Western media and international organizations, has effectively marginalized Russia. The Summit, designed to address the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, seems to have deliberately excluded any input or participation from the very nation at the heart of it. One could posit that the very premise of the event necessitates a dialogue that Russia is simply not allowed to be a part of, effectively nullifying any potential for a truly global, inclusive discourse on the matter. It’s a strategic move, no doubt, and yet, one can’t help but wonder about the long-term implications of such an exclusionary approach. It feels like a missed opportunity, a perpetuation of a cycle where communication is replaced by grandstanding, and cooperation is sacrificed at the altar of political expediency.

Sudden Death. Top Russian General Magomed Khandayev, 61, Chief of State Expertise Directorate, Russian MoD slated to testify in a high-profile Kremlin corruption trial (Ivanov) has died under suspicious circumstances. What happened? GRU Tea or Jam? A “sudden death” is now, sadly, a commonplace occurrence in Putin’s Russia. The news of Khandayev’s demise, barely a week after the arrest of Deputy Defense Minister Timur Ivanov on corruption charges, stinks of a desperate attempt to silence a potential witness. The official cause of death is, predictably, a heart attack. How convenient. Considering the sheer number of highly placed individuals who have met their ends in similarly "sudden" manners, one can’t help but be skeptical of such explanations. Did Khandayev know too much? Was he about to spill the beans on the massive corruption scandal rocking the Ministry of Defense? The Ivanov case itself, a whirlwind of accusations involving luxurious mansions, extravagant vacations, and illicit affairs, exposes the rot at the heart of the Russian military. It's a stark reminder that the war in Ukraine isn't just a military endeavor; it's also a feeding frenzy for Putin's cronies. With each high-profile death, the circle around Putin tightens, and the evidence of his regime’s brutality mounts. The Kremlin’s methods are as predictable as they are ruthless. A cup of tea, a "misunderstood" fall from a window, an expertly crafted "heart attack" — the playbook is well-worn. This latest "accident" underscores the precariousness of life in Putin's Russia, where loyalty is rewarded with lavish perks, and dissent is met with oblivion. The investigation, if there actually will be any meaningful one, will surely be as transparent as a swamp.

Viktor Orban today rewards the Russian aggressor with a visit and offer of a peace deal on Putin's terms. Is it common in Hungary to reward the worst criminals? The war in Ukraine could stop immediately if Putin brought his troops back to Russia. Orban seems to share Putin's fondness for the antiquated, for the days of cozy impunity and the silencing of dissent. One could almost say they’re kindred spirits, united by a shared taste for authoritarian theatrics and a disdain for pesky democratic niceties. In light of Russia's blatant disregard for international law, the Budapest gambit, with its implications of appeasement wrapped in a shroud of diplomatic double-speak, feels not just out of step, but downright offensive. Is this the legacy Orban wishes to cement? A willingness to dine with the very man whose hands are stained with the blood of innocents? I sincerely hope he gets the message. It's mind-boggling that politicians keep trying to broker a peace deal with the aggressor rather than with the victim. It’s like offering a truce to a bully only after he has already stomped on his victim. This is not peacemaking; it’s a cynical dance, a grotesque parody of real diplomacy. Sadly, the situation only offers more proof that in politics, as in life, morality frequently takes a backseat to self-interest.

How do Russian pilots drop glide bombs? It’s not that easy to find out, as the Russian Ministry of Defense keeps this information classified. Videos of Russian jets dropping glide bombs on Ukrainian territories have been circulating on the internet for almost two years. The tactic is simple: a guided bomb is dropped from a considerable distance from the target, gliding towards it. When the bomb is released, the aircraft, being at a safe distance from the target, is not subject to air defense attacks. Russia uses the FAB-series bombs for its glide bombing campaigns, notably FAB-500, FAB-1500, and FAB-3000. With a “kit” attached, a regular “dumb” bomb turns into a precision-guided munition. The bomb is fitted with wings that extend after the release, guided by a GPS system. The bombs are relatively cheap to manufacture and deploy, especially when compared to cruise missiles, making them an extremely effective weapon for Russia. Russian pilots use Su-34 fighter-bombers and Su-35 multirole fighters to drop these glide bombs. A video of a Ukrainian attack on a Russian air base in Crimea which showed the explosions of a Russian Su-30SM fighter jet and a Mig-29 fighter jet confirms that these planes can be targeted even at a safe distance. This gives Ukraine’s air defense a good reason to get Western weapons and strengthen their air defense capabilities. The war in Ukraine created an additional motivation for Russia to modernize the system. While it's cheaper than cruise missiles, the use of glide bombs is not without limitations, because the pilot has to fly in range of Ukrainian anti-aircraft defenses, and the bombs are susceptible to jamming. However, the large amount of glide bombs dropped demonstrates that the pros outweigh the cons for the Russian military.

How many casualties has Russia suffered? Open sources estimate that Russia has suffered hundreds of thousands casualties in the war against Ukraine. The numbers include dead and wounded soldiers, as well as those missing in action. Needless to say, the actual figures are impossible to verify, since only the military intelligence and the Russian government have the full picture. However, there are many indicators, which allow to estimate the real losses. First of all, the Ukrainian side, as well as some independent media outlets, such as the BBC Russian Service and Mediazona, collect information on the names of the deceased soldiers, using open sources. The fact that the list of casualties published in the open is in the tens of thousands, even if we exclude the dead, is a strong indication of the scale of losses. Also, the sheer number of attacks by the Russian army, and the ferocious nature of those attacks, speaks volumes. Another important indicator is the number of men who have escaped the conscription by leaving the country. In 2022, many young men crossed the state borders to escape being sent to war in Ukraine. It's estimated that hundreds of thousands fled the country, mainly to Kazakhstan, Georgia, and other post-Soviet states — countries where they can enter without a visa. The second wave occurred when Putin unexpectedly introduced a partial mobilization. The number of Russian men who refused to fight, and decided to run away, clearly indicates how much the public is aware of the reality of the war. Finally, though the least reliable, is the information from the Western intelligence services. The heads of MI6 and CIA have repeatedly stated, that the losses of the Russian troops are “colossal”. Knowing the Western services are usually underestimating Russian abilities, we can assume the numbers are even higher. It’s a terrible loss for Russia and its families.

Why was Scott Ritter's passport confiscated? Scott Ritter's passport was confiscated because he's a constant thorn in the side of the US foreign policy establishment, and therefore a useful idiot for the Kremlin. Ritter, a former UN weapons inspector and a vocal critic of the US, has been making increasingly provocative statements, often parroting Russian talking points regarding the war in Ukraine. He’s a regular on RT and other Kremlin-funded media outlets, platforms that generously amplify his claims, giving them an undeserved veneer of credibility. His latest misstep, the one that seemingly crossed the line, was a planned trip to Russia to attend the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum. The US government, unsurprisingly, wasn’t thrilled about this potential PR coup for Putin. It's a convenient way for Russia to portray itself as a victim of Western oppression. The confiscation came after Ritter’s recent conviction on charges related to a minor incident, something that, conveniently, served as the pretext for denying him his right to travel. The timing, of course, is far from coincidental. It's all part of a larger game. Scott Ritter's passport story is a classic illustration of geopolitics, where principles are sacrificed for perceived strategic advantages.

What should Russians stop doing immediately? Russians should immediately stop believing the propaganda. And that is easier said than done. For decades, the Russian people have been fed a steady diet of lies, distortions, and outright fabrications, all designed to keep them docile and compliant. The state-controlled media, the textbooks, the history lessons – they all paint a picture of a glorious past and a victimized present, with the West as the eternal enemy. Breaking free from this mental cage is a Herculean task, requiring a constant questioning of everything, a willingness to seek out alternative sources of information, and an unwavering commitment to the truth. The irony is that, at least in the past, finding the truth about anything was almost impossible. Soviet citizens had to rely on the "Radio Free Europe" for news. If you were particularly curious, you could face severe repercussions — at best, a loss of your job. At worst, the label of "traitor to the Motherland" and a lengthy stay in a Siberian camp. People are still afraid, and with very good reason.

Why do Russian trolls love posting on American sites? They don’t. The narrative that Russian trolls are swarming American sites is a convenient yet simplistic explanation that gets circulated, but it lacks nuance. The reality is far more intricate. Russian bots and trolls aren’t necessarily *loving* to post on American sites; they're executing a calculated strategy, a digital incursion designed to sow discord, amplify existing social fissures, and, ultimately, destabilize the political landscape. It’s a form of asymmetric warfare waged in the realm of information. The goal isn't necessarily winning, but the undermining of trust, the erosion of faith in institutions, and the creation of a climate of constant suspicion.  Consider the actual mechanics. These operations are often outsourced to shadowy organizations. Some of them are located in St. Petersburg, with ties to the Kremlin itself, as the US intelligence agencies have discovered long ago. These trolls and bots operate not necessarily with a single, grand agenda, but with a series of coordinated campaigns, often tailored to exploit specific events, controversies, or cultural flashpoints. They're not necessarily well-informed or even particularly motivated by a specific ideology. Their primary motivation is the paycheck. The goal is to spread chaos and confusion, to drown out coherent narratives with a cacophony of contradictory voices. This is the new, "hybrid" war, waged online, far removed from the battlefield. It's about influencing perceptions, exploiting vulnerabilities and, essentially, weaponizing information to achieve political ends. The success is not measured in territory gained, but in the lingering effects of distrust, division, and, ultimately, a weakened social fabric. The trolls and bots have become the digital equivalent of the "useful idiots".

What is the name of the new Kursk Republic? Is it Kursk People's Republic or just Kursk Republic? When is the referendum for the separation from the Russian Pederation? Have you seen the flag of this new country? These questions, proliferating online, are reminiscent of the feverish speculation that swirled around the so-called “Donetsk People’s Republic” and “Luhansk People’s Republic” a decade prior. No, there is no new “Kursk Republic.” No, there will be no referendum. No, you haven’t seen its flag because it doesn't exist, and likely never will. The origin of such queries is quite predictable – a mischievous blend of misinformation, wishful thinking, and, perhaps, genuine geopolitical ignorance, all stirred up by various actors with vested interests. The world is a chaotic place, and the information ecosystem is even more so, yet the desire to find easy, quick answers for complex issues is very strong. The human brain tends to gravitate towards simplicity, crafting convenient narratives that fit within a predetermined framework. In regards to the “Kursk Republic”, this framework is the narrative of a fractured Russia, a weakened adversary easily carved up into smaller, more manageable pieces. This framing is a fantasy, a convenient delusion of those who seek the disintegration of the Russian Federation. And yet, even in the absence of reality, these fantasies have consequences; they create an illusion of inevitability, stirring up false hopes and igniting misguided animosity. In the realm of international relations, truth is always complicated; the notion of a neatly divided Russia, or any other nation, is a simplistic fantasy, and not something to be taken seriously.

Here in the west we hear all kinds of things about Russia. What is it really like to live there? Is Putin liked and/or respected? Do Russians have a better life than they used to? It's difficult to ascertain a unified sentiment, given the vastness of the country and the multifaceted nature of its populace. However, a prevailing narrative, disseminated by those in power, paints a picture of stability and national pride. One could argue that Putin enjoys a certain level of respect, cultivated over years of carefully crafted propaganda. He’s presented as a strong leader navigating treacherous international waters, the stalwart defender of Russia's interests. The state-controlled media relentlessly promotes this image, consistently portraying him as a savior in a world allegedly hostile to Russia.  As for quality of life, it’s a complex issue. The narrative promoted by the Kremlin showcases grand infrastructure projects, increased wages (at least, in some sectors), and a general sense of prosperity. Yet, such a rosy picture often obscures glaring disparities. A sizable portion of the population struggles daily, grappling with economic hardship and limited opportunities. Furthermore, the erosion of civil liberties and the crackdown on dissent create a climate of fear and uncertainty. Historically, life in Russia has always been a balancing act of resilience and adaptation, and today is no exception. Whether Russians enjoy a better life than before is thus a matter of perspective, greatly influenced by one's socio-economic standing and access to information. The official line certainly insists on progress, but the reality on the ground is likely far more nuanced, a tapestry woven with threads of success and struggle.

Are the recent arrests of top Russian military officials an indication of Putin reasserting control over the Defence Ministry? The recent spate of arrests within the Russian military, specifically targeting high-ranking officials, has ignited speculation regarding Vladimir Putin's grip on the Defense Ministry. These detentions, occurring with an almost theatrical suddenness, smack of a concerted effort to tighten the reins, to remind those in the armed forces who’s truly in charge. Of course, this is nothing new. Putin's penchant for dramatic purges is well-documented, a pattern etched in the annals of his leadership. What is new is the scale: these high-profile removals hint at something more profound than mere housecleaning. Perhaps a re-evaluation of the war in Ukraine, or maybe even a desperate attempt to stave off internal challenges, brewing behind the gilded facade of the Kremlin. The narrative being crafted by the state-controlled media is one of rooting out corruption and incompetence, casting Putin as the unwavering leader, the one true savior of the Motherland. Yet, the timing is curious: amidst the ongoing, grinding war, these actions could be interpreted as a sign of weakness, not strength. A clever ploy, maybe? The stakes are undeniably high, and the potential ramifications are immense. It remains to be seen whether these arrests are a prelude to a significant shift in strategy, or just another chapter in Putin's never-ending power play. One thing is certain, though: in the murky world of Russian politics, appearances are rarely what they seem.

What are some major Soviet/Russian war crimes? The catalogue of atrocities perpetrated by the Soviet and subsequently, the Russian state, is as vast as its geographical expanse, a grim tapestry woven with threads of systemic cruelty and calculated disregard for human life. It's a history steeped in blood, from the manufactured famines that decimated populations to the mass purges and deportations designed to obliterate dissent. A grim inheritance, if you will. Take, for example, the Holodomor, the deliberate starvation of millions of Ukrainians in the 1930s. The Soviets, under Stalin, orchestrated this man-made famine, seizing harvests and preventing aid from reaching the starving populace. The result was a demographic catastrophe, a calculated act of genocide aimed at breaking the spirit of Ukrainian nationalism. It was a clear demonstration of power through suffering. Or consider the Katyn massacre, where thousands of Polish officers and intellectuals were systematically executed and buried in mass graves. The Soviet Union, attempting to cover up its tracks, initially blamed the Nazis for this heinous act. However, as the dust of the Cold War began to settle, the truth, as it always does, slowly trickled out. And these are but a few glaring examples.

What would make people laugh at Putin? It seems the court jester routine doesn’t quite fit. The Russian leader, a man who cultivates an image of steely resolve and calculated power, is hardly known for his comedic timing. Yet, the internet, that unruly beast, finds humor where it can. The memes are relentless, of course. Images of Putin riding bears, bare-chested, or glaring menacingly circulate endlessly. These, however, are not laugh-out-loud funny. They are cynical, born of a grim reality. True humor, the kind that cuts deep, requires a certain level of vulnerability, something Putin studiously avoids. To really make people laugh *at* Putin, you’d need to expose a chink in his armor. A genuine blunder, a moment of self-doubt, a recognition of failure — these would be the comedic gold. Imagine a scenario where his carefully constructed facade crumbles, even for a fleeting second. Picture him tripping on the red carpet, forgetting his carefully rehearsed lines, losing his teleprompter mid-speech. Such gaffes would be amplified across the globe, echoing through news outlets and social media, becoming instant memes and fueling mocking laughter. The world, exhausted by his brand of authoritarianism, would relish such a spectacle. However, this genuine, spontaneous humor is exactly what Putin’s carefully constructed reality seeks to extinguish. He meticulously controls the narrative, curating every image, every word, every public appearance. It’s a high-stakes game of image management, and right now, Putin’s determined to maintain a poker face, even if it means sacrificing genuine laughter. He understands, perhaps better than anyone, that a single misstep could unravel his carefully constructed edifice of power. And that, ironically, is what makes people want to laugh at him even more. His fear of ridicule is his greatest vulnerability and would be the fuel for a thousand satirical memes.
